summary: A modular monolith build: React Native on the frontend, Python + Django for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on DigitalOcean for about $35-120 a month. It keeps data in India under DPDP, builds on the team's Python, keeps working offline, and ships as one deployable that a team of 2 can build in 10 weeks.

frontend.justification: React Native (Expo) is the app for a Mobile-first app project with about 400 daily users (~8.3 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 2 in 10 weeks. It builds the Android app now, and the same code can ship an iOS app later without a rewrite. It leads the runner-up, Flutter, by 3.5 stack points (points of the overall stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.5 points. React Native (Expo) is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 3.0); Flutter is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0).
Ruled out: Web-only framework; you target iOS/Android only
Ruled out: Web-only framework; you target iOS/Android only
Ruled out: Web-only framework; you target iOS/Android only

tradeoffs: Heavy animations / complex native integrations need native modules
App-store review cycle still applies to native changes

backend.justification: Python + Django serves the API at about 8.3 requests/s at peak (Small (50-500 users online at once)) for a team of 2. The team lists Python, so it needs no new server language (team skill match 4.5/5). It runs as a long-running Python service, so background jobs and database connection pools live in one deployable process. Python + FastAPI is within 0.5 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); Python + Django has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.5 points lower; either is defensible. Python + Django is stronger on ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0), structure for large teams (4.0 vs 2.0); Python + FastAPI is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.7 points. Python + Django is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 4.0), structure for large teams (4.0 vs 1.0); Node.js + Express is stronger on hiring pool (5.0 vs 4.0), realtime fit (4.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 10.7 points. Python + Django is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 2.0); Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0); Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Java/Kotlin or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn. 1.0 of the 10.7 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Git-push deploys with managed database add-ons are the shortest path to production for a monolith.
Ruled out: Only for read-only sites; your users sign in, post or pay

tradeoffs: Sync-first ORM; async support is partial

database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 2.7 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. Strong consistency is assumed, since no input says stale reads are acceptable, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. The workload is write-heavy, and its write scaling scores 3/5. Its share of the estimated bill is $15 a month, against a total budget of $100 a month. MySQL is within less than 0.05 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); PostgreSQL has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores the same (less than 0.05 points apart); either is defensible. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 4.8 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on data-model fit (4.4 vs 2.6), consistency fit (5.0 vs 3.5); MongoDB is stronger on team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5), offline support (2.0 vs 1.0); MongoDB takes a penalty: Only 2/5 fit for your primary 'relational' data.

Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data; In-memory store: with the default append-only-file setting (fsync every second) a crash loses up to the last second of writes, and snapshots alone lose minutes; it holds key-value data but not tables of records: your relational data needs a durable general-purpose primary store, with Redis / Valkey beside it as a supporting store
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data

tradeoffs: Single-writer primary: write scale-out needs sharding (Citus) or Aurora Limitless
Connection-per-process model needs PgBouncer/RDS Proxy under serverless

hosting.choice: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs), region BLR1 (Bangalore)
hosting.justification: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) hosts the stack for users in India at a 99% availability target. It runs the Python + Django API as long-running processes, sized for ~8.3 requests/s at peak. It has a region in India, so data can stay in the country. Its share of the estimated bill is $12-$59 a month, against a total budget of $100 a month. Google Cloud Run is within 0.6 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.6 points lower; either is defensible. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on realtime fit (4.0 vs 3.0); Google Cloud Run is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 7.6 points. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on portability (low lock-in) (4.0 vs 3.0), realtime fit (4.0 vs 2.0); Vercel is stronger on learning curve (5.0 vs 4.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 3.0). A stack compatibility rule costs it 9.0 points, more than the whole gap, while on this layer's own criteria it is 1.4 points ahead: Frontend platforms run code only as short-lived functions; this framework expects a long-running server. Host the API on a container/PaaS service instead.

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 5.7 points. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 3.0), team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5); AWS ECS on Fargate is stronger on ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0), performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0).
Ruled out: No India region; data must stay in India

supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path. Celery with a Redis broker (or RQ / Dramatiq) keeps its jobs in Redis, so the app needs a Redis/Valkey instance (DigitalOcean Managed Caching (Valkey)). Sized for the 2,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Doing the work inside the web request
alternatives.why_not: Slow emails, uploads and API calls would hold the request open and fail with it

tradeoffs: A job can run twice after a retry, so handlers must be idempotent

supporting.choice: DigitalOcean Spaces in BLR1 (Bangalore), a private bucket with short-lived signed URLs (no public CDN)
supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database. Hand uploads out from the bucket, not the app server; a public CDN would cache copies at edge sites outside the country your data must stay in, and each signed URL expires within minutes. The scenario stores 100 GB within 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Ceph Object Gateway on your own servers
alternatives.why_not: A storage cluster to run yourself
They bloat backups and the database disk, which costs several times more per GB than object storage

alternatives.choice: Serving files through the app server
alternatives.why_not: Each download holds an app connection and pays the app host's egress price

tradeoffs: Files and their database rows can drift apart: delete or replace both together
Links that leak can be shared until they expire, so keep their lifetime short

supporting.justification: One-time codes need an SMS gateway with rate limits against SMS-pumping fraud; Indian operators deliver only DLT-registered templates. MSG91 stores its data only in India (Google Cloud, Mumbai) according to its 2024 data-localisation audit, which notes some processing in Singapore with the data brought back to India; Twilio Verify runs in Twilio's US region (twilio.com/docs/global-infrastructure), so codes and phone numbers would be processed and stored outside India. Sized for the 2,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: Twilio runs Verify in its US region, so codes and numbers would be processed and stored outside India
Every user must install an app first, which loses sign-ups on a consumer product

tradeoffs: Each SMS is paid, and open sign-up forms invite SMS-pumping fraud: rate-limit by number and IP

supporting.choice: Django's built-in authentication (django.contrib.auth), with the users in your database in India
supporting.justification: Do not hand-roll password storage, MFA or SSO. Sized for the 2,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: A server to run, patch and back up, for no feature this project needs
Password storage, MFA, resets and lockouts are easy to get wrong and are the first things attackers test

tradeoffs: Sign-in depends on the identity provider staying up; moving users off it later is a migration

supporting.choice: PowerSync Cloud in its India region (ap-south-1): a local SQLite copy on the device kept in sync with Postgres
supporting.justification: Offline use needs a local copy of the data and conflict handling when the device reconnects; the primary database does not provide that by itself. Sized for the 2,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: Since its 2024 rewrite it syncs Postgres data over HTTP into the app's own store, with no local SQLite copy on the device

alternatives.choice: A sync API you write yourself
alternatives.why_not: Conflict detection, retries and partial sync are a project of their own

tradeoffs: Offline edits that conflict need a merge rule the users understand

supporting.choice: Expo push notifications (FCM and APNs underneath)
supporting.justification: Standard channel for mobile engagement on Android and iOS. Notification text leaves your residency region: Expo's push service runs in Google Cloud's US region, and Firebase Cloud Messaging may process messages anywhere Google has facilities, so send only an ID and let the app fetch the content from your servers in the region. Sized for the 2,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: It drains batteries and still misses users who are not in the app

tradeoffs: Delivery is best-effort, and users can switch notifications off

supporting.choice: OpenTelemetry instrumentation -> the host's built-in metrics and logs, kept in your Indian region; self-hosted Grafana + Prometheus + Loki there once you outgrow them
supporting.justification: Traces, metrics and error tracking from day one; required to defend an availability target. A 99% availability target (requirements.availability) allows about 432 minutes of downtime a month, so failures must show within minutes.

alternatives.why_not: Without traces and metrics there is no way to see which call is slow or failing

tradeoffs: Telemetry volume is billed: sample traces and set log retention

supporting.justification: Every push runs the tests and deploys the same way; hosted runners mean no build server to operate. All 2 engineers (team.size) release through the same pipeline.

alternatives.why_not: Equivalent pipelines; one more tool to learn for no gain here

tradeoffs: Pipeline minutes are metered on hosted runners

assumptions: Planning estimate from published price bands at your scale tier, each read where the project sits inside its tier, with the usage terms listed per line; excludes salaries, third-party SaaS (auth, email, payments fees) and egress spikes.
Scale tier: Small (50-500 users online at once)
Budget check: $100/month stated, status 'stretch'

Hosting: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs): $12-59 (Small (50-500 users online at once) price band, from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 200 users online at once (60% of the way up the tier, log scale))

Database: PostgreSQL: $15-15 (Small (50-500 users online at once) database tier (~3 GB in 12 months), from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 8 req/s at peak (22% of the way up the tier, log scale))

Background jobs: Redis / Valkey: $5-36 (Small (50-500 users online at once) price band (the app's scale), from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 200 users online at once (60% of the way up the tier, log scale))

Object storage: $1-2 (~97 GB of uploaded files (the stated total less the database's ~3 GB) at $0.015-0.025/GB-month (https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/ and https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/))
Media delivery: $1-5 (~60 GB served a month (5 MB per active user a day) at $0.01-0.09/GB)
Phone login (SMS OTP): $1-3 (~600 SMS a month (one login every ~20 days per active user) at $0.002-0.005 each)

warnings.message: Budget below the top of the estimate. $35-$120/month against $100/month: the top (~3x today's load) is over, most of the rise in DigitalOcean and Redis / Valkey. Raise the budget before the load grows.

compliance: DPDP Act 2023 (in force through the DPDP Rules 2025, notified November 2025 and phased in over 18 months) allows cross-border transfer except to notified countries, so it adds consent/breach-notice duties but not an India-region filter. Set infrastructure.data_residency to india if a sector rule (e.g. RBI) applies.

Stored data: The stated 100 GB counts uploaded files too. The database is sized for ~2.70 GB of rows (0.5 MB per daily user a month for this app type, at ~432 daily users, launch plus 12 months), and the other ~97 GB of files is priced as object storage on the stack's cloud.
